title: Vote early in person or by mail (absentee voting)
question: How can I vote early in person or by mail in Charlottesville, and what are the deadlines?
office: Office of Voter Registration and Elections (General Registrar)
summary: Any registered Charlottesville voter may vote absentee without giving a reason, early in person or by mail. Early voting needs no application and runs from 45 days before the election (for November 3, 2026 the city opened Friday, September 18) until 5:00 p.m. on the Saturday before, at the City Hall Annex office; bring ID or sign an ID Confirmation Statement. To vote by mail, apply online or on the state form so the office receives it by 5:00 p.m. on the 11th day before the election (October 23, 2026). Return the ballot by 7:00 p.m. on Election Day, or postmarked by Election Day and received by noon on the third day after. A defect on a ballot received by the Friday before the election can be cured until noon on the third day after.

legal_basis.quote: Any registered voter may vote by absentee ballot in accordance with the provisions of this chapter in any election in which he is qualified to vote.
Each electoral board shall meet in the month of May or June in 2007, and every four years thereafter, and shall appoint a general registrar
Absentee voting in person shall be available on the forty-fifth day prior to any election and shall continue until 5:00 p.m. on the Saturday immediately preceding the election.
An application shall not be required for any registered voter appearing in person to cast an absentee ballot pursuant to § 24.2-701.1 .
Except as provided in subsection F, a registered voter voting by absentee ballot in person shall provide one of the forms of identification specified in subsection B of § 24.2-643 .

If he does not show one of the forms of identification specified in subsection B of § 24.2-643 , he shall be allowed to vote after signing a statement, subject to felony penalties for false statements pursuant to § 24.2-1016 , that he is the named registered voter he claims to be.

For purposes of this chapter, such offices shall be open to the public (i) a minimum of eight hours between the hours of 8:00 a.m. and 5:00 p.m. on the first and second Saturday and (ii) a minimum of five hours between the hours of 11:00 a.m. and 5:00 p.m. on the second and third Sunday immediately preceding all elections.
Any applicant who is in line to cast his ballot when the office of the general registrar or voter satellite office closes shall be permitted to cast his absentee ballot that day.

Not later than 55 days prior to any election, the general registrar shall post notice of all voter satellite office locations in the locality and the dates and hours of operation of each location in the office of the general registrar and on the official website for the county or city.

An application for an absentee ballot may be accepted the later of (i) 12 months before an election or (ii) the day following any election held in the twelfth month prior to the election in which the applicant is applying to vote.

Any other application may be made by mail, by electronic or telephonic transmission to a facsimile device if one is available to the office of the general registrar or to the office of the Department if a device is not available locally, or by other means.
The application shall be made to the appropriate registrar no later than 5:00 p.m. on the eleventh day prior to the election in which the applicant offers to vote.
The applicant's printed name and the last four digits of the applicant's social security number.

An application that is completed in person at the same time that the applicant registers to vote shall be held and processed no sooner than the fifth day after the date that the applicant registered to vote
Any registered voter shall be eligible to file a special application to receive absentee ballots for all elections in which he is eligible to vote.

The application for an absentee ballot shall provide space for the applicant to indicate that he will require assistance to vote his absentee ballot by reason of blindness, disability, or inability to read or write.

the general registrar shall not reject the application of any individual because of an error or omission on any record or paper relating to the application, if such error or omission is not material in determining whether such individual is qualified to vote absentee.

The general registrar shall make printed ballots available for absentee voting not later than 45 days prior to any election or within three business days of the receipt of a properly completed absentee ballot application, whichever is later.
An envelope, properly addressed and postage prepaid, for the return of the ballot to the general registrar by mail or by the applicant in person, or to a drop-off location.

After the voter has marked his absentee ballot, he shall (a) enclose the ballot in the envelope provided for that purpose, (b) seal the envelope, (c) fill in and sign the statement printed on the back of the envelope, (d) enclose the ballot envelope and any required assistance form within the envelope directed to the general registrar, and (e) seal that envelope.

A mailed absentee ballot shall be returned (i) by mail to the office of the general registrar, (ii) by the voter in person to the general registrar, or (iii) to a drop-off location established pursuant to § 24.2-707.1 .
Failure to follow the procedures set forth in this section shall render the applicant's ballot void.
On the day of the election, there shall also be a drop-off location at each polling place in operation for the election.

Not later than 55 days prior to any election, the general registrar shall post notice of the sites of the drop-off locations in the locality in the office of the general registrar and on the official website of the county or city.
Any voter who is in line to return an absentee ballot at a drop-off location by 7:00 p.m. on the day of the election shall be permitted to deposit his absentee ballot.

any absentee ballot (i) returned to the general registrar after the closing of the polls on election day but before noon on the third day after the election and (ii) postmarked on or before the date of the election shall be counted pursuant to the procedures set forth in this chapter if the voter is found entitled to vote.

Within three days of such finding, the registrar shall notify the voter in writing or by email of the error or failure and shall provide information to the voter on how to correct the issue so his ballot may be counted.

The voter shall be entitled to make such necessary corrections before noon on the third day after the election, and his ballot shall then be counted pursuant to the procedures set forth in this chapter if he is found to be entitled to vote.
For any absentee ballot received by the Friday immediately preceding the day of the election
the polls shall be open at each polling place at 6:00 a.m. on the day of the election and closed at 7:00 p.m. on the same day
Any person who has applied for and received an absentee ballot may choose not to vote absentee and shall be entitled to cast a ballot in accordance with the provisions of this subsection.

Any person who has applied for and has been sent an absentee ballot but does not receive the ballot or loses the ballot shall be entitled to cast a ballot in accordance with the provisions of this subsection.

A person with a disability or illness who has applied for and has been sent an absentee ballot who did not receive or has lost the absentee ballot on or before the Saturday before the election may obtain a replacement absentee ballot.

Any person registered and otherwise qualified to vote may request at any time prior to 2:00 p.m. on the day preceding the election that he be permitted to vote by emergency absentee ballot with the assistance of his designated representative.

A qualified voter may vote absentee in person in the office of the general registrar through 2:00 p.m. on the day immediately preceding the election by complying with the requirements of § 24.2-643 and affirming that one of the following emergency circumstances will prevent him from voting on election day:

After 12:00 p.m. on the Saturday before the election, an obligation arose that requires the voter be absent from his county or city on election day for (i) his business, profession, or occupation; (ii) the hospitalization of the voter or a member of his immediate family; or (iii) the death of a member of his immediate family.
The Secretary, in coordination with local election officials, shall implement a free-access system by which a voter may determine:

The electoral board of each county and city shall send a written explanation of the reason for rejection of an absentee ballot to the voter whose absentee ballot is rejected within 90 days of the date on which the ballot is rejected.

An officer of election, by a written notice given to the voter, shall inform him that a determination of his right to vote shall be made by the electoral board and advise the voter of the beginning time and place for the board's meeting and of the voter's right to be present at that meeting.
A central absentee voter precinct shall be made by the governing body by ordinance; the ordinance shall state for which elections the precinct shall be used.
The circuit courts shall have jurisdiction to issue an injunction to enforce the provisions of this section upon the application of (i) any aggrieved voter

The State Board, through the Department of Elections, shall supervise and coordinate the work of the county and city electoral boards and of the registrars to obtain uniformity in their practices and proceedings and legality and purity in all elections.

Any willfully false material statement or entry made by any person in any statement, form, or report required by this title shall constitute the crime of election fraud and be punishable as a Class 5 felony.
The following omissions are always material and any Envelope B containing such omissions shall be rendered invalid if any of the following exists:
The voter did not provide the voter's birth year; or
The voter omitted the date, or provided an incorrect or incomplete date on which the voter signed Envelope B;

If there is no evidence from the Intelligent Mail barcode that the ballot was mailed after the close of polls for the relevant election and if the return envelope has a missing postmark, the ballot shall be rendered invalid.

steps.step: Make sure you are registered to vote at your Charlottesville address
steps.how: Check your registration on the Virginia Citizen Portal or by calling the Office of Voter Registration and Elections. Absentee ballots come from the registrar of the locality where you are registered. The city's Register to Vote page warns that its borders with Albemarle County are confusing (the Albemarle registrar's number, 434-972-4173, is on the city's elections page), and its voter FAQ notes that the University of Virginia and PVCC are mostly in Albemarle. If you register in person and apply for a mail ballot at the same time, the application is processed no sooner than the fifth day after you registered.
steps.deadline: For the November 3, 2026 election the city lists the close of books as October 23, 2026 (registration rules are in the voter registration process)
steps.quote: Voters can check their registration status using the online Citizen Portal or by calling our office.

steps.step: Choose how to vote absentee: early in person, or by mail
steps.how: No reason is needed for either. Voting early in person needs no application. Voting by mail needs an application for each election, unless you join the permanent absentee list, which sends you a ballot for every election you are eligible to vote in.
steps.quote: As of July 1, 2020, voters no longer need a reason to apply for a mail ballot.

steps.step: Early in person: go to the Office of Voter Registration and Elections during the early voting period
steps.how: Early voting is at the Office of Voter Registration and Elections, City Hall Annex, 120 7th St. NE, Room 142 (no satellite office is listed). For the November 3, 2026 general election the office is open for early voting Monday through Friday from September 18 to October 30, 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.; on Saturdays October 24 and 31, 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.; and on Sundays October 18 and 25, 12:00 p.m. to 5:00 p.m. Anyone in line when the office closes may still vote that day. The city recommends voting in the first three weeks to avoid longer lines. Paid parking is in the Market Street Garage, with street parking beside the Annex.
steps.deadline: Early voting ends at 5:00 p.m. on the Saturday before the election (October 31, 2026 for the November 3, 2026 election)
steps.quote: Voting will begin Friday, September 18 at the office and will continue, Monday through Friday, until Friday, October 30, from 8:30AM-4:30PM.

steps.step: Early in person: give your name and address, show ID or sign an ID Confirmation Statement, and vote
steps.who: Voter; officers of election and the registrar's staff at the office
steps.how: Give your name and residence address. Show an acceptable ID (the city's FAQ lists, for example, a Virginia driver's license, a U.S. passport, a student ID from a Virginia college, or a current utility bill or bank statement with your name and address; an out-of-state driver's license is not accepted), or sign the ID Confirmation Statement. A voter who does neither is offered a provisional ballot. Then vote as you would at your precinct; an accessible ballot marking device is available. Curbside voting from your car is available to anyone with a disability or limited mobility, or over the age of 65 (the city gives 434-970-3250 for questions). If you vote a provisional ballot because you had no ID and did not sign the statement, see the escalation for the electoral board's deadline.
steps.quote: If he does not show one of the forms of identification specified in subsection B of § 24.2-643 , he shall be allowed to vote after signing a statement, subject to felony penalties for false statements pursuant to § 24.2-1016 , that he is the named registered voter he claims to be.

steps.step: By mail: apply for a mail ballot
steps.how: Apply online through the Virginia Citizen Portal (this needs a Virginia DMV-issued ID), or complete the paper Virginia Absentee Ballot Application (SBE-701/703.1) and send it to the Office of Voter Registration and Elections by mail (P.O. Box 1219, Charlottesville, VA 22902), by fax (434-970-3249), by email to vote@charlottesville.gov (a scan or clear photo), or in person. You can also call the office to have a paper application mailed to you. The application needs your name, the last four digits of your Social Security number, your registration address, the address the ballot should go to if different, and your signature. Say on the form if you need help marking the ballot. Answer Yes in Section 4 to join the permanent absentee list. Applications may be accepted from 12 months before the election (or from the day after an election held in that twelfth month, if later); the city asks voters to apply early. The Citizen Portal shows whether the application was received and accepted.
steps.deadline: Received by 5:00 p.m. on the 11th day before the election (October 23, 2026 for the November 3, 2026 election)
steps.quote: We must receive your application no later than 5 PM eleven days prior to the election.

steps.step: By mail: the registrar reviews the application and mails the ballot
steps.who: General Registrar (Office of Voter Registration and Elections)
steps.how: The registrar notes whether you are a registered voter in Charlottesville. An error or omission that is not material to whether you are qualified cannot be a reason to reject the application. State law requires ballots to be available no later than 45 days before the election, or within three business days of receiving a properly completed application, whichever is later; the city says ballots start going out about 45 days before the election. The mailing holds the ballot, Envelope B with the Statement of Voter, a postage-prepaid return envelope and instructions that list the drop-off locations, plus an assistance form if you asked for help. The city says that if you apply after early voting has begun, expect the ballot within 7 to 10 business days of the office receiving the application.
steps.deadline: Ballots made available no later than 45 days before the election, or within three business days of receiving a properly completed application, whichever is later
steps.quote: The general registrar shall make printed ballots available for absentee voting not later than 45 days prior to any election or within three business days of the receipt of a properly completed absentee ballot application, whichever is later.

steps.step: By mail: track your application and ballot
steps.how: The Virginia Citizen Portal shows whether your application was received and accepted. Once the ballot is mailed, follow it with Ballot Scout (linked from the city's Ballot Scout page). If the ballot does not arrive in time, contact the office at (434) 970-3250 or vote@charlottesville.gov.
steps.quote: Once your ballot has been mailed, you can follow its progress through the United States Postal Service by using Ballot Scout.

steps.step: By mail: mark the ballot and complete Envelope B
steps.who: Voter (and an assistant, if you asked for help)
steps.how: Mark the ballot privately and seal it in Envelope B. Fill in and sign the Statement of Voter on Envelope B: your full name, your residence address, the last four digits of your Social Security number and your birth year. A missing signature, first or last name, house number and street, both city and ZIP code, birth year or last four digits makes the ballot invalid unless it is cured (the cure process covers ballots received by the Friday before the election; see s10); a missing middle name or a missing or wrong date does not. If you asked for assistance, complete and sign the assistance form sent with the ballot and return it with the ballot (the city's Early Voting page says to complete, sign and return it whether or not assistance was needed). Put Envelope B (and any assistance form) in the return envelope and seal it.
steps.quote: After the voter has marked his absentee ballot, he shall (a) enclose the ballot in the envelope provided for that purpose, (b) seal the envelope, (c) fill in and sign the statement printed on the back of the envelope, (d) enclose the ballot envelope and any required assistance form within the envelope directed to the general registrar, and (e) seal that envelope.

steps.how: Mail it in the postage-prepaid return envelope, hand deliver it to the Office of Voter Registration and Elections, or put it in the 24-hour City of Charlottesville Official Ballot Drop Box directly outside the office (open from September 18, 2026). On Election Day there is also a drop-off location at each polling place. State law allows three ways to return a mail ballot: by mail (which includes a commercial delivery service), by the voter in person to the registrar, or at a drop-off location.
steps.deadline: Received at the office or a drop-off location by 7:00 p.m. on Election Day, however it is returned (anyone in line at a drop-off location at 7:00 p.m. may deposit the ballot); a mailed ballot that arrives later counts only if postmarked on or before Election Day and received by noon on the third day after (Friday, November 6, 2026 for the November 3, 2026 election). Under 1VAC20-70-20(F), a mailed ballot arriving after Election Day with a missing postmark is invalid, and one with an illegible postmark is checked against its mail barcode and the Envelope B date, so mail it early.
steps.fee: None: the return envelope is postage prepaid
steps.quote: Your ballot must be hand delivered by 7:00 PM on Election Day or postmarked by the day of the election and received in the office by noon on the following Friday.

steps.step: If the registrar finds a problem with your returned ballot, correct it (cure)
steps.who: General Registrar notifies; the voter corrects
steps.how: For a ballot received by the Friday before the election, if the Statement of Voter was not filled out correctly or completely, or a required step was missed, and the error would make the ballot void, the registrar records the issue and tells you in writing or by email how to fix it. The registrar may issue a new ballot. Contact the office promptly.
steps.deadline: The registrar notifies within three days of finding the problem; the voter corrects it before noon on the third day after the election (Friday, November 6, 2026 for the November 3, 2026 election)
steps.quote: Within three days of such finding, the registrar shall notify the voter in writing or by email of the error or failure and shall provide information to the voter on how to correct the issue so his ballot may be counted.

steps.step: If your mail ballot never arrives, is lost or damaged, or you change your mind, vote in person instead
steps.who: Voter; General Registrar or officers of election; a designated representative (replacement ballot)
steps.how: Lost or never arrived: before Election Day, give the registrar (or an officer of election) a signed statement that the ballot did not arrive or was lost, then vote a regular ballot; on Election Day, you may vote at your polling place or the central absentee voter precinct, but only a provisional ballot. Unused or damaged ballot: before Election Day, return it to the registrar (unopened, or opened and unmarked; a damaged ballot is marked spoiled) and vote a regular ballot at the office, or vote at your polling place on Election Day (a regular ballot if the officers can confirm the return, otherwise a provisional ballot); or bring it to your polling place on Election Day and vote a regular ballot. Without the unused ballot on Election Day you vote a provisional ballot. A voter with a disability or illness whose ballot did not arrive or was lost by the Saturday before the election may instead request a replacement ballot by close of business that Saturday, through a designated representative (18 or older, not an elected official, a candidate, or the deputy, spouse, parent or child of one) who collects it and returns it by the close of polls, on the State Board's form. Polls are open 6 a.m. to 7 p.m.
steps.deadline: Early voting at the office ends at 5:00 p.m. on the Saturday before the election; a replacement ballot (Va. Code § 24.2-703.2) must be requested by close of business that Saturday and returned by the close of polls; polls are open 6 a.m. to 7 p.m. on Election Day
steps.quote: Any person who has applied for and has been sent an absentee ballot but does not receive the ballot or loses the ballot shall be entitled to cast a ballot in accordance with the provisions of this subsection.

steps.step: In an emergency after the deadline, ask for an emergency absentee ballot
steps.who: Voter; a designated representative; General Registrar
steps.how: Use the Emergency Absentee Ballot Application (ELECT-705) if (i) you could not apply by the deadline because of your hospitalization or illness, the hospitalization, illness or death of your spouse, child or parent, or another emergency; (ii) such an emergency arising after the application deadline will keep you from voting on Election Day; or (iii) you applied in time, your ballot had not arrived within 10 days of the election, and such an emergency will keep you from voting on Election Day. You sign the form in front of your designated representative (18 or older, and not an elected official, a candidate, or the deputy, spouse, parent or child of one), who signs it and returns it to the office. The registrar gives the ballot to the representative, who delivers it, watches you mark and seal it, and returns it to the office. Separately, if after 12:00 p.m. on the Saturday before the election an obligation arose that requires you to be away from the city on Election Day for your business, profession or occupation, your own or an immediate family member's hospitalization, or a death in your immediate family (or you are an officer of election assigned after that time to another precinct), you may vote in person at the office through 2:00 p.m. on the day before the election, showing ID or signing the ID Confirmation Statement.
steps.deadline: Request before 2:00 p.m. on the day before the election; the completed form returned by 5:00 p.m. that day; the ballot counts only if the registrar receives it before the polls close
steps.quote: Any person registered and otherwise qualified to vote may request at any time prior to 2:00 p.m. on the day preceding the election that he be permitted to vote by emergency absentee ballot with the assistance of his designated representative.

steps.step: After the election: if your absentee ballot was rejected, you receive a written reason
steps.how: If an absentee ballot is not counted, the electoral board must send the voter a written explanation of the reason. You can also check the ballot's status on the Citizen Portal. No appeal of a rejected ballot was found in the sections read (see escalation for the cure and other routes).
steps.deadline: Within 90 days of the date the ballot is rejected
steps.quote: The electoral board of each county and city shall send a written explanation of the reason for rejection of an absentee ballot to the voter whose absentee ballot is rejected within 90 days of the date on which the ballot is rejected.

escalation.trigger: Mail ballot application not accepted (for example, the last four digits of the Social Security number or the signature are missing)
escalation.next: General Registrar: send a corrected application before the deadline, or vote early in person instead (no application needed)
escalation.deadline: 5:00 p.m. on the 11th day before the election for a mail ballot; 5:00 p.m. on the Saturday before the election for early voting in person
escalation.quote: the general registrar shall not reject the application of any individual because of an error or omission on any record or paper relating to the application, if such error or omission is not material in determining whether such individual is qualified to vote absentee.

escalation.trigger: Returned mail ballot has a defect that would make it void (for example, no signature, birth year or last four Social Security digits on Envelope B)
escalation.next: General Registrar (cure: correct the Statement of Voter, or vote a new ballot the registrar issues)
escalation.deadline: Before noon on the third day after the election
escalation.quote: The voter shall be entitled to make such necessary corrections before noon on the third day after the election, and his ballot shall then be counted pursuant to the procedures set forth in this chapter if he is found to be entitled to vote.

escalation.trigger: Mail ballot never arrived or was lost
escalation.next: General Registrar before Election Day (signed statement, then a regular ballot), or the polling place on Election Day (provisional ballot, decided by the Charlottesville Electoral Board)
escalation.deadline: Statement before Election Day; or at the polls on Election Day, 6 a.m. to 7 p.m.
escalation.quote: The voter may, prior to the day of the election, present to the general registrar or officer of election a statement signed by him that he did not receive the ballot or has lost the ballot.

escalation.trigger: Requested ballot not received within 10 days of the election, and the voter's hospitalization or illness, the hospitalization, illness or death of a spouse, child or parent, or another emergency will keep the voter from the polls
escalation.next: General Registrar: emergency absentee ballot delivered through a designated representative
escalation.deadline: Request before 2:00 p.m. on the day before the election; form returned by 5:00 p.m. that day
escalation.quote: has applied to receive an absentee ballot by the deadline but has not received his ballot within 10 days of the election and will be unable to vote on election day due to his hospitalization or illness, the hospitalization, illness, or death of a spouse, child, or parent, or other emergency found to justify receipt of an emergency absentee ballot.

escalation.trigger: Voted a provisional ballot (for example, at early voting without showing ID or signing the ID Confirmation Statement)
escalation.next: Charlottesville Electoral Board, which decides whether the provisional ballot counts; any provisional voter may attend the board's meeting, and a voter who voted provisionally for lack of ID may send a copy of ID or a signed statement by fax, email, in person or mail
escalation.deadline: ID or signed statement received by the electoral board no later than noon on the third day after the election
escalation.quote: to be received by the electoral board no later than noon on the third day after the election.

escalation.trigger: Unhappy with how the office handled an application, a ballot or a visit
escalation.next: Office of Voter Registration and Elections, or the Charlottesville Electoral Board (which appoints the General Registrar, Va. Code § 24.2-110(A), and meets the second Wednesday of every month unless posted otherwise), by email, phone or in writing
escalation.quote: Please file your suggestion or complaint with the Office of Voter Registration or the Charlottesville Electoral Board via email, by phone, or in writing.

escalation.trigger: The registrar does not process an application or send a ballot as the law requires
escalation.next: Circuit court, presumably the Charlottesville Circuit Court (injunction to enforce Va. Code § 24.2-706, on the application of an aggrieved voter; the statute does not name the venue)
escalation.quote: The circuit courts shall have jurisdiction to issue an injunction to enforce the provisions of this section upon the application of (i) any aggrieved voter

escalation.trigger: The local office or electoral board does not follow election law
escalation.next: Virginia Department of Elections and the State Board of Elections, which supervise local electoral boards and registrars (the Department's contact page links a Virginia Voters' Election Day Complaint Form; under § 24.2-103(E) the State Board may also begin removal proceedings against a general registrar)
escalation.quote: The State Board, through the Department of Elections, shall supervise and coordinate the work of the county and city electoral boards and of the registrars to obtain uniformity in their practices and proceedings and legality and purity in all elections.

caveats: Start date: Va. Code § 24.2-701.1(A) makes early voting available on the 45th day before an election. For November 3, 2026 that is Saturday, September 19, but the city's notice opens early voting on Friday, September 18, and the city's Polling Places page and voter FAQ say early voting begins the 46th day before the election. The reason for the earlier start was not found in the sources read.

Witness: the city's Early Voting page tells mail voters to return the ballot once the envelope is signed and witnessed, but in the same text says a witness is not required to open the ballot. The Statement of Voter in Va. Code § 24.2-706(C)(2) (index text) asks for the signature, the last four digits of the Social Security number, the birth year and the date, with no witness line, and 1VAC20-70-20(B) lists the birth year and last four digits (not a witness) as material. Follow the instructions mailed with the ballot.

Versions: the index marks Va. Code §§ 24.2-653, 24.2-706, 24.2-709, 24.2-709.1 and 24.2-711.1 "effective until January 1, 2027" and § 24.2-653.01 "effective September 1, 2026, until January 1, 2027", and § 24.2-703.1 (permanent absentee list) "effective until July 1, 2027", and holds no successor text. They govern the November 3, 2026 election; re-check the deadlines, the cure process and the permanent absentee list for elections from 2027.

Broken link: the Early Voting page's "Virginia Vote By Mail Application (PDF)" link (https://www.elections.virginia.gov/media/formswarehouse/absentee-voting/applications/SBE-701-703.1.pdf) answered HTTP 404 on 2026-10-10. The city's main elections page and the Department of Elections link the working form (f1).

Email: the directory and the Early Voting page give vote@charlottesville.gov; the "email" link in the candidates section of the main elections page points to vote@charlottesville.org. The .gov address is recorded.

Tracking: the city's Ballot Scout page embeds https://v2.ballotscout.org/charlottesville-city/search, its Quick Links point to a ballotscout.org partner page, and the Department of Elections page links https://ballot.elections.virginia.gov/voter/va/bt/track. None of these lookup tools was opened (they ask for voter details).

Stale city text: the voter FAQ still says registration records close 21 days before an election and describes absentee eligibility for students in terms of an excuse. Va. Code § 24.2-416(A) in the index closes the records during the 10 days before a general election, which matches the city's October 23, 2026 close of books. The main elections page says no reason has been needed since July 1, 2020, and Va. Code § 24.2-700 has no excuse requirement.

Local law: Va. Code § 24.2-712(A) requires the city to set up its central absentee voter precinct by ordinance, and § 24.2-701.2 lets it create voter satellite offices by ordinance. The City Code (published on Municode, whose terms were not confirmed as allowing reuse) was not read, no city page cites a City Code section on absentee voting, and no local ordinance is quoted. The city's notice cites only Va. Code §§ 24.2-701.2(E) and 24.2-707.1(C).

Rejected applications: no statute read requires the registrar to notify an applicant whose mail ballot application is rejected, and no appeal route for a rejected application or a rejected ballot was found. The routes recorded are a corrected application or in-person voting, the cure process, the electoral board's written explanation after the election (§ 24.2-711.1(B)), complaints to the office, the electoral board or the Department, and an injunction under § 24.2-706(G).
Cure coverage: the notice duty in § 24.2-709.1(C) covers ballots received by the Friday before the election; how the office handles defects on ballots received later was not found.
Fees: no source read states a fee for applying for or voting an absentee ballot, and none appears on the city pages; the fees recorded are the prepaid return postage and the free status system.

Hours: the dates and hours recorded are from the city's public notice for the November 3, 2026 general election; other elections have their own notices. The early voting and drop box details for other elections should be read from the city's notice, which state law requires 55 days before each election.

Not modeled: military and overseas (UOCAVA) voters, who may apply on the Federal Post Card Application and get ballots by email or fax, with a later return deadline (§§ 24.2-702.1, 24.2-703, 24.2-709(C)); and the screen-reader ballot for print-disabled voters (§ 24.2-704(B)), which the city describes on its main elections page.

Charlottesville Electoral Board: no separate office channel for the board was found; the city FAQ directs complaints to the office or the board by email, phone or in writing, and the main elections page gives its regular meeting day.

Replacement ballots: Va. Code § 24.2-703.2 lets a voter with a disability or illness whose ballot did not arrive or was lost get a replacement through a designated representative, on a form the State Board prescribes. Neither the city pages nor the Department's absentee page read links that form, so no form is recorded; ask the office.

Postmarks: 1VAC20-70-20(F) makes a mailed ballot that arrives after Election Day invalid if the postmark is missing, and checks an illegible postmark against the mail barcode and the Envelope B date. The city pages do not mention this.

Court: Va. Code § 24.2-706(G) gives "the circuit courts" jurisdiction but does not name the venue; the Charlottesville Circuit Court is inferred for a Charlottesville voter, and its clerk's office line and address are recorded.
Names: the city pages and the circuit court page name office holders; no names are recorded here.

corrections: Quotes: all 65 original quotes confirmed. The 55 state-law quotes are substrings of I.text_of for the cited section (whitespace normalised only), and each subsection label matches the text. The 6 city step quotes and the FAQ escalation quote were matched against /396/, /431/ and the voter FAQ (served at /m/faq?cat=55) re-fetched on 2026-10-11; the 3 quotes from 1VAC20-70-20 were matched against law.lis.virginia.gov re-fetched the same day. Five quotes were added and checked the same way: Va. Code §§ 24.2-709.1(C) (cure covers ballots received by the Friday before), 24.2-603 (poll hours), 24.2-703.2 (replacement ballots), 24.2-705(B)(1) (late-arising obligations) and 1VAC20-70-20(F)(3) (missing postmark).
Summary: 'Defects can be cured by then' overstated the cure. Under § 24.2-709.1(C) the notice-and-cure process covers ballots received by the Friday before the election; the summary now says so.

s6: the law requires ballots to be available 'not later than 45 days prior' (§ 24.2-612), not from 45 days before. The deadline and the step text now say 'no later than', and the city's 'about 45 days' is given as the city's statement. 'Checks that you are registered' is now 'notes whether you are a registered voter' (§ 24.2-706(B)).

s8: the list of material omissions now matches 1VAC20-70-20(B): it adds missing both city and ZIP code and says house number and street rather than 'street address'. 'Unless it is cured' now says that the cure covers ballots received by the Friday before the election. Adds the full name and residence address to the Statement of Voter items (§ 24.2-706(C)(2)) and the city's instruction to return the blue assistance form whether or not help was needed.

s9: the deadline read as if a mailed ballot always needs an Election Day postmark. Any ballot received by 7:00 p.m. on Election Day counts (§ 24.2-709(A)); the postmark rule applies only to mailed ballots arriving later (§ 24.2-709(B)). Adds the missing-postmark rule of 1VAC20-70-20(F).
s10: adds the condition in § 24.2-709.1(C) that the error or failure 'would render the ballot void by law'.

s11: the draft mixed up the Election Day rules. The 'unless the officers can confirm the return' rule applies to an unused or damaged ballot returned to the registrar before Election Day (§ 24.2-708(A)(1), (C)(1)); a voter whose ballot never arrived or was lost votes only a provisional ballot on Election Day (§ 24.2-708(B)(2)). The step now separates the two cases and names the central absentee voter precinct. Adds the replacement ballot for voters with a disability or illness (§ 24.2-703.2), with its Saturday request deadline, which was missing.

s12: 'a death in the family' was broader than § 24.2-705(A), which names the hospitalization, illness or death of a spouse, child or parent, or another emergency, and clause (ii) needs an emergency that arose after the application deadline. The 705(B) route now gives the conditions of § 24.2-705(B)(1) (an obligation arising after 12:00 p.m. on the Saturday before, requiring absence from the city on Election Day, and the officer-of-election case) and the ID requirement of § 24.2-643. The escalation rung for a ballot not received within 10 days uses the same family wording.

s5: 'Applications are accepted from 12 months before' is now 'may be accepted', with the later-date rule of § 24.2-701(A). s4: the curbside phone number is given as the city's line for questions, which is how the Early Voting page gives it.

s1: the 'borders are confusing' statement is on the city's Register to Vote page (/455/), which was not in the sources; the source is added and the step names that page. The Albemarle registrar's office line, listed on the city's elections page, is added to contacts for voters who find they are registered in Albemarle.

Form f4 (SBE-703.1C): fillable was null. The PDF's AcroForm has an empty Fields array, so it is recorded as not fillable. Form numbers, revisions and titles for f1, f3, f4 and f5 were confirmed from the PDFs; the Early Voting page's SBE-701-703.1.pdf link still answers 404.

Escalation: the provisional-ballot rung said any provisional voter may send ID; under § 24.2-653(B) that applies to a voter who voted provisionally for lack of ID, while any provisional voter may attend the meeting. The court rung now says that § 24.2-706(G) does not name the venue, and a caveat records the inference.

Caveats: adds the July 1, 2027 end date of § 24.2-703.1, the 10-day close of books in § 24.2-416(A), the missing-postmark rule, the replacement ballot form that was not located, and the court venue inference.
open_issues: No local ordinance is quoted: the central absentee voter precinct ordinance required by § 24.2-712(A) was not read (the City Code is on Municode, whose terms were not confirmed). It does not change any voter step.
The State Board form for a § 24.2-703.2 replacement ballot was not located on the pages read.
The city's Early Voting page still says the envelope is 'signed and witnessed', while §§ 24.2-706(C)(2) and 24.2-707(A) in the index and 1VAC20-70-20 have no witness requirement; recorded in caveats.
Sections 24.2-653, -653.01, -706, -709, -709.1 and -711.1 end on January 1, 2027, and § 24.2-703.1 on July 1, 2027; the index holds no later text. This does not affect the November 3, 2026 election.
